newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: POLL-Australian bond juggernaut to skid year-end.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Australian bond juggernaut to skid year-end.

text.p: This year's impressive rally in Australian bonds is expected to show signs of waning by the end of 1997 as economic growth finally gets into full swing.
But for now the rally remains on course, not least because this week's key inflation and wages data could trigger another monetary policy easing, the fifth in this business cycle.

A Reuters poll of economists taken on Friday showed a median forceast for the 10-year bond yield at the end of 1997 at 7.05 percent, although estimates were fairly wide-ranging from 6.25 to 8.00 percent.
This compares with a current yield of just above 6.50 percent, around its lowest level in 3-1/2 years.
"Whenever bond yields in Australia are under 7.0 percent that are cruising for a bruising," Access Economics analyst Chris Richardson told Reuters Financial Television.
"It probably won't happen in the short-term, but towards the end of 1997 or early 1998 I can certainly see yields heading reasonably rapidly in the other direction," he added.
The performance of the market so far this year has outpaced all expectations, and largely reflects the failure of the economy to fire on all cylinders.

This is despite the inducement of easier monetary conditions in the past year with the Reserve Bank having lopped 200 basis points off official interest rates since last July to its current level of 5.5 percent.

Also fuelling the rally from just over 8.0 percent since April has been a rebound in U.S. Treasuries on signs of a pause in U.S. economic demand and the possibility that a further policy tightening by the Federal Reserve is not warranted just yet.
"Cut off any of these essential nutrients for the current rally and the local bond yield would back-up very fast," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

While the local market's rally has been impressive in outright terms, so has its comparative performance against the United States, and on a 10-year yield differential it now stands at its lowest level since the early 1980s.
Reuters also polled economists as to where they saw the Australian/U.S. 10-year spread at the end of the year which produced a median of 50 basis points over.
This compares with a current level of just over 30 b.p., but again expectations were wide, from 120 b.p. over to a negative spread of 50 b.p.

With yields set to rise towards the end of 1997 as the local economy fires up and concerns over tighter monetary policy begin to stir, so will the spreads widen, but some economists expect the margin can go tighter and possibly negative before the trend reverses.
However, analysts at Deustche Morgan Grenfell expect the spread to breach parity and stay there with the market outperforming a declining U.S. market on Australia's far-superior inflation outlook.
Indeed this week's second quarter Australian headline Consumer Price Index is expected to produce an annual rate of just 0.5 percent, well below that of the U.S. at 2.3 percent.
Underlying inflation is also expected to be well below the Reserve Bank's 2.0-3.0 percent rate at 1.7 percent.

"Given the inflation outlook is so good for the next two, maybe three quarters at least, the Reserve Bank clearly is over-achieving on its inflation target," Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Australia, told RFTV.
"With the unemployment rate at 8.5 percent, I think it makes it very hard for them not to cut interest rates once more. But I think once more is all they can do," Pease added.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
